title: GEN AI IN PROOF-BASED MATH COURSES: A PILOT STUDY
extended_summary:
This pilot study investigates how generative AI is used and perceived in advanced proof-based undergraduate mathematics courses, with particular attention to whether AI can support learning without undermining mathematical reasoning. The paper responds to growing concerns about widespread student use of generative AI, the unreliability of AI detection tools, and the need for course policies that promote learning and critical thinking rather than simple prohibition. The authors focus on understanding how students in proof-based mathematics courses engage with AI, what they find helpful or problematic, and what these patterns imply for instruction.

The intervention was not an AI tutoring system designed by the researchers, but rather a course policy that explicitly permitted generative AI use, specifically Microsoft Copilot through university accounts, across assignments and assessments. Students were required to critically evaluate AI outputs, justify solutions, and cite textbook theorems and definitions by number. Data were collected at the end of the semester through a 26-question Qualtrics survey and follow-up semi-structured Zoom interviews. The study therefore examines students’ real-world use of an allowed AI tool under structured classroom expectations rather than comparing AI versus non-AI conditions.

The context was three asynchronous online, upper-level proof-based mathematics courses at Indiana University East in spring 2025: Introduction to Modern Algebra I, Introduction to Modern Algebra II, and Introduction to Topology. The participant pool consisted primarily of undergraduate students, with 19 survey responses from 17 undergraduate students and 4 interviews; graduate students in a combined graduate algebra topics course were invited but provided no responses. The courses were taught within a small regional commuter campus where many students were part-time, non-traditional in age, and able to complete mathematics degrees fully online.

The main conclusions are that students used generative AI in varied and cautious ways, often for concept clarification, brainstorming, recalling definitions, checking work, or improving wording rather than directly producing complete proofs. Students generally found Copilot helpful as a supplemental learning aid, but they also reported that it was often inaccurate for advanced proof-writing and required careful verification. AI use did not appear to reduce interaction with instructors, though it had mixed effects on peer discussion, with some students feeling discussions improved and others feeling that AI-generated posts reduced authenticity. The authors conclude that generative AI may have value in proof-based mathematics when framed as a tool for exploration and critique, but its educational benefit depends on guided, critical use that reinforces rather than replaces independent reasoning.

identified_tools.name: Microsoft Copilot
identified_tools.description: Microsoft Copilot is a generative AI assistant integrated with Microsoft services; in this paper it was the university-approved GenAI tool students could use through Indiana University accounts.
identified_tools.use_case: Students in three asynchronous proof-based undergraduate mathematics courses were allowed and encouraged to use Microsoft Copilot for first drafts of homework, concept explanations, brainstorming, checking proofs, recalling definitions/results, and drafting discussion posts, with required verification and citation of course theorems/results.

findings.finding_summary: In this mixed-methods pilot, students generally perceived Microsoft Copilot as helpful for learning proof-based mathematics, especially for understanding concepts, retrieving information, brainstorming approaches, and checking work. However, students also reported that Copilot often struggled with complex problems and complete proofs, and perceptions of its effect on independent problem-solving were mixed across the 19 survey responses from 17 students.
findings.measure: Student self-reported perceived helpfulness for learning and independent problem-solving in proof-based mathematics courses (survey responses and interviews)

findings.finding_summary: Students reported that using Microsoft Copilot sometimes supported critical thinking by forcing them to verify outputs, detect errors, and 'debug' flawed proofs. At the same time, some students worried that reliance on the tool could reduce ownership of solutions and compromise the learning process in pure mathematics.
findings.measure: Student self-reported critical evaluation, reasoning, and perceived effects on ownership/independent thinking from survey and interview data

findings.finding_summary: Students reported nuanced effects of Microsoft Copilot on engagement and peer interaction. The paper states that Copilot did not generally reduce engagement with instructors, but students were split on its effect on interactions with classmates; some felt discussions improved, while others felt AI-generated posts reduced authenticity and human connection.
findings.measure: Student self-reported engagement with instructors and classmates, including perceptions of discussion quality and authenticity

findings.finding_summary: Students generally found Microsoft Copilot easy and intuitive to use in the course context, reporting minimal onboarding challenges. The authors note that this ease of use likely supported adoption as a regular learning aid, though some students suggested a short instructor demonstration would improve use.
findings.measure: Student self-reported ease of use and ease of evaluating Copilot responses

findings.finding_summary: Students were consistently cautious about Microsoft Copilot's reliability for advanced proof-based mathematics, frequently identifying inaccuracies and emphasizing the need to verify outputs. The paper reports that Copilot could be 'wildly inaccurate' for proofs and abstract concepts, limiting trust in rigorous mathematical contexts.
findings.measure: Student self-reported perceptions of reliability and accuracy of AI outputs for proofs and abstract mathematical concepts

quality_tier_rationale: This is a small mixed-methods pilot study based on voluntary end-of-semester surveys and interviews, with no randomized or quasi-experimental design and mostly self-reported outcomes. The evidence is exploratory and qualitative/descriptive rather than causal.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports mixed, perception-based outcomes with no effect sizes or objective achievement gains. Benefits were reported for understanding and ease of use, but reliability concerns and mixed effects on independent problem-solving and peer interaction make overall impact unclear.
